displayQuote: He who says he can and he who says he can't are both usually right

meta.title: Who really said "He who says he can and he who says he can't are both usually right"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Confucius — nothing like it exists in the Analects, in Legge's English or in the Chinese. It is a 'he who' rewrite of the saying credited to Henry Ford, which is itself an old proverb: 'They can, because they think they can' was printed in 1718.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'He who says he can and he who says he can't are both usually right'?
meta.ogDescription: Not in the Analects, and no Chinese exists for it. It is the Henry Ford line in fancy dress — and Ford's own claim to it is a 1947 magazine attribution printed after he died.

answer.label: Not Confucius — a dressed-up version of an old English proverb
answer.authorDates: Anonymous proverb · the idea in print by 1718, the Ford wording by 1940
answer.sourceLine: There is no Analects source and, decisively, no Chinese text — the Analects is 20 books and about 500 numbered passages, all searchable in the original, and nothing of this sense appears in any of them. What you are reading is the saying usually credited to Henry Ford: ‘Whether you think you can, or think you can’t — you’re right.’ And that one has a twist too. It is an old proverb Ford probably never said: Joseph Trapp put it into English in 1718, translating Virgil — ‘They can, because they think they can.’

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: 子曰：「由！誨女知之乎！知之為知之，不知為不知，是知也。」
trail: We searched all twenty books of the Analects in Chinese and in James Legge’s public-domain English. Nothing of this sense occurs. The nearest passage is a different lesson entirely — Book II, on knowing what you know — and it is about intellectual honesty, not self-belief Book II in Chinese and Legge ↗.

The English saying has a documented lineage, and it is long. 1718: Joseph Trapp’s translation of the Aeneid gives ‘They can, because they think they can’ for Virgil’s possunt quia posse videntur. 1821: The Christian Guardian prints ‘if you think you can, you can.’ 1914: a baseball manager tells the Pittsburgh Press, ‘If you think you can, you can. If you think you can’t, you can’t’ the full chain ↗.

The modern both-halves-are-right wording turns up on a 1940 Iowa State locker-room sign: ‘If you think you can, you can; if you think you can’t, you’re right.’ That is the sentence on this page, minus the Confucian costume — and it was anonymous gym-wall wisdom.

As for Ford: the earliest attribution to him that researchers have found is in Reader’s Digest in September 1947, five months after he died, with no documentation that he ever said it. So the ‘real’ author of the Confucius quote turns out to be another misattribution — which is a nice illustration of how these things stack.
source.cutTag: Analects, Book II — the nearest passage
source.excerptNote: This is what Confucius does say in the neighbourhood, from Book II. Legge: ‘You, shall I teach you what knowledge is? When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it — this is knowledge.’ Note the direction of travel. He is telling a student to stop overclaiming; the modern quote tells you to claim more.

source.rightsNote: The genuine material on this page is free to reuse: the Chinese Analects is ancient, and James Legge’s English translation (1861–1893) is long out of copyright, so quote either without worry. The modern saying is a different matter but a simpler one — a proverb of unknown authorship in circulation for three centuries is not anyone’s property to license. What you should not do is reproduce it with Confucius’s name attached, which is a factual problem rather than a legal one. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Confucius
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Confucius
author.metaLine: 551–479 BC · Chinese teacher and philosopher (here, the misattributed figure)
author.bio: Confucius (Kong Qiu, 551–479 BC) taught in the state of Lu, and what we have of him is the Analects — a compact collection of remarks and exchanges assembled by his students after his death. It is short, it is complete, and it has been indexed for two thousand years, which makes it one of the easiest bodies of quotation on earth to check. That is exactly why misattributions to him are so unusually cheap to disprove: if a saying is his, there is Chinese for it, and someone can point you to the book and the passage. If there is only English, you already have your answer.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Two misattributions in one sentence, stacked. The Confucius credit is recent and baseless; the Henry Ford credit underneath it is older, more respectable, and also wrong.

items.why: Nothing of this sense appears in any of the twenty books of the Analects, in Legge’s English or in the original. The ‘he who…’ construction is the giveaway: it is a Victorian English translator’s cadence that modern fakers imitate to make a sentence sound Chinese search the Analects ↗.

Ford’s version, ‘Whether you think you can, or think you can’t — you’re right,’ is first tied to him in Reader’s Digest in September 1947, five months after he died. No speech, interview or book of his has been produced the 1947 attribution ↗.

1718, Trapp’s Virgil: ‘They can, because they think they can.’ 1821, The Christian Guardian. 1905, a school superintendent’s speech. 1914, a baseball manager. 1940, a locker-room sign that reads almost word for word like this quote. The saying was public property long before it had a famous name.

‘When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it’ (Legge). Confucius is curbing a confident student. The modern saying is a pep talk. They are not versions of each other.

We found no datable first instance, and Wikiquote’s Confucius page does not list it among the misattributions. Present circulation is social media, which suggests it is recent — but that is an inference, and we are not going to print a date we cannot source.

misattribution.truthLine: Not Confucius: there is no Chinese for it and nothing like it in the Analects. It is the Henry Ford saying rephrased — and even Ford’s claim rests on a magazine attribution printed after his death the trail ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is a motivational poster that sounds like a law of nature, and the symmetry does the work — both men are right, so the outcome must be inside them. Attach a 2,500-year-old name and the pep talk gets the authority of an observation.

The tell is the syntax. ‘He who…’ is not Chinese; it is nineteenth-century missionary English, the cadence Legge and his contemporaries used, and it has become the standard costume for any aphorism someone wants to make sound ancient. When you meet a ‘he who’ quote with no chapter number, assume the costume is all there is.
detailsBody: 1718: Joseph Trapp’s Aeneid — ‘They can, because they think they can,’ for Virgil’s possunt quia posse videntur.
1821: The Christian Guardian — ‘if you think you can, you can.’
1905: Walter D. Wintle’s poem ‘Thinking’ is published — ‘If you think you are beaten, you are’ — later reprinted, unattributed, in Napoleon Hill’s Think and Grow Rich (1937).
1914: a baseball manager, in the Pittsburgh Press — ‘If you think you can, you can. If you think you can’t, you can’t.’
1940: an Iowa State locker-room sign — ‘if you think you can’t, you’re right.’
September 1947: Reader’s Digest credits the saying to Henry Ford, five months after his death. The Confucius credit arrives later still, undated.
context.pull: 'He who' is not Chinese. It is Victorian missionary English — the standard costume for a fake.
